newsitem.title: JAPAN: Self-serve stations seen fuelling Japan price war.
newsitem.headline: Self-serve stations seen fuelling Japan price war.

text.p: Self-service gasoline stations are not expected to start rapidly emerging on Japan's roadsides even if a ban on allowing such sites is lifted, oil industry sources said on Tuesday.
But the added competition from even a few could fuel an already vicious price war, they said.

"Self-service stations are not expected to increase rapidly after the ban is lifted, but such stands will pressure retail prices," said Toshinori Itoh, a senior analyst with Daiwa Institute of Research (DIR).

Under a three-year programme which started in April 1995, the Fire Defence Agency is studying the safety aspects of self-service stations, and will come up with a decision on whether to approve them by the end of March 1998.

Japan now has about 60,000 stations, but analysts expect that to fall to about 38,000 by 2005 due to the continuation of a price war which was triggered by the deregulation of oil product imports in April 1996.
The average retail price of gasoline fell to a historic low of 105 yen per litre late last year, about 13 percent down from April 1994. Tax accounts for over half of the retail price.
Oil industry sources widely believe current restrictions will be eased, paving the way for self-service stations, which have been prohibited for safety reasons.
Jiro Izumi, an analyst with Yamaichi Research Institute, said self-service stations could probably sell gasoline for about 10 yen a litre less than full-service stations.
"However, the impact on prices is likely to be limited as the number of self-service stations is not expected to expand quickly," Izumi said.
Itoh said self-service pumps could eventually account for only only 10 percent of Japan's gasoline stations.
Analysts said the number of self-service stations was not expected to increase sharply, partly because profitability was questionable due to the high cost of land and equipment needed.
The current price war would also undermine the competitiveness of self-service stations, they said.
Oil industry sources said self-service stations require more land than normal sites because there will be no attendants to guide drivers to the pumps.
In city and suburban areas, drivers are swamped by gasoline station attendants who wipe windows, clean ashtrays and guide cars in and out of cramped sites.
Oil firms, suffering sharp downturns in profits because of the price war, are divided on the viability of self-service stations.
"The safety and environmental aspects of self-service stations could cause problems," a spokesman for Nippon Oil Co Ltd said.
Refiner Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd gave a more positive view.
"We aim to serve a wide range of customers, and would like to satisfy the needs of drivers who want full service and those who require minimum service," an Idemitsu spokesman said.
